digest.top_line: MASTERPLAN: adding SBRT 40Gy/5fx to mFOLFIRINOX-based CT cut 12mth LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (p=0.022) in high-risk operable, BRPC or LAPC pancreas.
digest.tldr: Upper GI led: SBRT added to induction CT lowered LRR in randomised phase II MASTERPLAN, while IO added to dCRT failed twice in esophageal/GEJ cancer (KEYNOTE-975 EFS HR 0.97 in CPS ≥10; ARION 12-mo cPFS 48.6% vs 48.9%). Bone-met pain: PALEM embolization 52.5% 72-h response in RT-ineligible pts; FURTHER MR-HIFU missed primary at 69/129 accrual.

sites.intro: Non-EBRT options for painful bone mets: embolization in RT-ineligible pts, and an underpowered MR-HIFU vs EBRT RCT.

studies.name: PALEM
studies.tldr: Arterial embolization gave 72-h pain relief in 52.5% (62/118; 95% CI 43.1-61.8%) of RT-ineligible painful bone mets, with no primary safety events.
details: 🔍 Multicenter single-arm prospective confirmatory study, N=120 enrolled, J-SUPPORT policy

subdetails: RT-ineligible, or ≥8 weeks after prior RT
Most painful lesion embolized with microspheres, no anticancer drug

details: 🔍 Response defined by international consensus criteria for palliative RT trials (BPI-SF item 3 + morphine-equivalent dose)
📐 Efficacy test one-sided α=0.025, power 0.9, assumed 40% response
🔍 Safety event = any CTCAE G≥4 or G≥3 CNS necrosis through day 14
⚠️ Only 72-h response reported in source; durability of relief unknown
⚠️ Response includes stable pain with lower opioid dose; component breakdown not reported in source
⚠️ Lesion sites, histologies and vascularity not reported in source

verdict.rationale: Single-arm, no RT or analgesic comparator; met both prespecified thresholds, but 72-h endpoint only and no durability data in source.
verdict.audience: Painful bone mets, pain ≥5 on analgesics, RT-ineligible or ≥8 wk post-RT

studies.significance: The response definition comes from the palliative RT consensus criteria, so the 52.5% reads on an RT-style scale, but at 72 h, earlier than RT response is usually assessed. The population is RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks post-RT, so this is an option when re-irradiation is off the table, not a substitute for first-line palliative RT.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts with painful bone mets who are RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks past prior RT, this supports considering embolization for rapid relief; it does not extend to RT-naive pts eligible for palliative RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter, **single-arm**, prospective confirmatory hypothesis-assessment study under J-SUPPORT policy; protocol published. **N=120** enrolled; UMIN000040794.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Painful bone metastases on analgesics with **pain score ≥5**, either **RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks after prior RT**. Most painful lesion treated.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Arterial embolization of tumor-feeding vessels with microspheres, **without anticancer drugs**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Co-primary: **immediate efficacy** at 72 h (BPI-SF item 3 plus morphine-equivalent dose, per palliative RT consensus criteria) and **safety** (CTCAE G≥4 or G≥3 CNS necrosis through day 14). Overall success required both.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Both co-primary endpoints met; **52.5% pain relief** against a 26% null, and **no primary safety events** in 119 pts.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Palliative EBRT remains the standard for painful bone mets; PALEM tested no RT arm, and borrowed the RT consensus response definition, so the scale is shared but the timepoint and population are not.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with painful bone mets on analgesics who cannot receive RT or are ≥8 weeks past prior RT. Does not represent RT-naive pts eligible for palliative RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Response counts unchanged pain with reduced opioid as success, which can inflate a 72-h rate. Lesion site, histology and late outcomes not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Shows embolization clears a prespecified efficacy bar quickly with a clean early safety profile. Does not settle durability, retreatment, or how it compares with re-irradiation or SBRT in the post-RT setting.

studies.interpretation:
The design choice that matters most for an RT reader is the endpoint. PALEM defined response using the international consensus criteria built for palliative RT trials, combining the worst-pain item of the BPI short form with daily morphine-equivalent dose. That makes the 52.5% rate legible to anyone who has read the palliative RT literature, but it is not directly comparable to it. Radiation response under those criteria is usually assessed weeks after treatment, once the biological effect has had time to appear. PALEM measured at 72 h, which is the whole argument for embolization: speed. A reader should take the result as evidence that a meaningful fraction of pts get relief within days, not as evidence that embolization matches or exceeds RT on the scale RT trials use.

The population defines where this fits. Eligibility required either RT ineligibility or at least 8 weeks since prior RT, so the trial was built for the pt whom the radiation oncologist has already treated or cannot treat. In that setting the realistic alternatives are re-irradiation, SBRT for a previously treated site, analgesic escalation, or other interventional procedures. PALEM compared against none of them. The 26% null threshold was set against a background of no effective rapid option, which is reasonable for a single-arm confirmatory design but means the trial establishes that embolization works, not that it is the best choice for the post-RT pt.

The composite response definition deserves scrutiny. Success included reduced pain with unchanged opioid, reduced pain with reduced opioid, and unchanged pain with reduced opioid. The third category is the softest: a pt whose pain did not move but whose opioid dose dropped at 72 h counts as a responder, and in an unblinded single-arm study opioid adjustment is partly a clinician decision. The source does not break the 62 responders down by category, so it is not possible to say how much of the rate rests on pain reduction itself.

The safety result is cleaner. No CTCAE grade 4 events and no grade 3 or higher CNS necrosis in 119 pts, with an upper confidence bound of 3.1% against a 15% ceiling, is reassuring for a procedure that embolizes vessels near the spinal cord in some sites. The window was only 14 days, though, and the source does not report lesion location, so the reader cannot tell how many spinal or pelvic lesions sit behind that number.

What would change the read is durability. A 72-h response that fades by week 4 is a bridge, useful while waiting for RT effect or for a pt with very short life expectancy. A response that holds would make embolization a standalone option for the RT-exhausted site and a plausible partner to RT for pts who need relief before radiation can work. The obvious next trial is embolization followed by RT versus RT alone in RT-eligible pts, with both the early and the conventional consensus timepoints.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Response used the palliative RT consensus criteria but at 72 h, so the 52.5% shares RT's scale without matching its timepoint. Eligibility was RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks post-RT, positioning embolization beside re-irradiation for the previously treated site rather than against first-line palliative RT.

open_questions: Durability of pain relief beyond 72 h?
Embolization vs re-irradiation for previously treated sites?
Embolization plus RT vs RT alone in RT-eligible pts?

studies.name: FURTHER
studies.tldr: 2-wk pain response 50% vs 38% (p = 0.41) for MR-HIFU ± EBRT vs EBRT alone; primary not met, trial accrued 69 of 129 planned.
details: 🔍 Multicenter 1:1:1 RCT, six European hospitals, enrolled 2020-2025
🔍 Arms: MR-HIFU vs EBRT vs EBRT followed by MR-HIFU within one week
🔍 Painful (NRS ≥ 4) non-spinal bone mets, eligible for both EBRT and MR-HIFU
🔍 Excluded: life expectancy <3 months, (impending) fracture, curative intent
📊 2-wk pain response (BPI pain score + opioid use): MR-HIFU ± EBRT 50% vs EBRT 38%, p = 0.41
⚠️ Accrual 69 of 129 target despite 2-yr extension (COVID-19, low MR-HIFU eligibility)
⚠️ Primary pools MR-HIFU and combination arms vs EBRT; no per-arm 2-wk response in source
⚠️ 2-wk primary favors the fast-onset modality: authors cite 4-6 wk for EBRT effect
⚠️ EBRT dose and fractionation not reported in source
⚠️ EBRT 6-wk response 47%, below the 70% EBRT benchmark the authors cite
🔍 Bayesian reanalysis to offset low power promised at ESMO; not in source

verdict.rationale: Primary missed at 69/129 planned accrual; pooled HIFU arms vs EBRT on a 2-wk endpoint that favors fast onset. Combination benefit is a secondary, unpowered signal.
verdict.audience: Painful non-spinal bone mets, NRS ≥ 4, eligible for EBRT and MR-HIFU

studies.significance: The RT signal sits in the combination arm: pain response rose 26% → 81% from wk 1 to wk 6 with EBRT then MR-HIFU, vs 35% → 47% with EBRT alone. EBRT dose was not reported, so transfer to a single-fraction practice can't be checked. The decision in play is adding MR-HIFU to EBRT, not replacing EBRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts with painful non-spinal bone mets for whom EBRT is no longer an option, this supports MR-HIFU as an alternative; it does not establish MR-HIFU over EBRT as first-line palliation, and excluded spinal lesions and (impending) fracture.

primary_endpoint.name: Pain response at 2 weeks
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: MR-HIFU ± EBRT vs EBRT, p = 0.41, not met

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter **1:1:1 randomized** trial across six European hospitals, enrolled 2020-2025. **69 randomized** against a target of 129; accrual fell short despite a 2-yr extension.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with good/reasonable performance and **painful (NRS ≥ 4) non-spinal bone mets**, eligible for both EBRT and MR-HIFU. Excluded life expectancy <3 months, (impending) fracture, or curative intent.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: EBRT alone, or EBRT followed by MR-HIFU **within one week**. **Dose and fractionation not reported in source.**

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** pain response 2 wk after start of treatment, from BPI pain score and opioid use. Secondary: pain scores and pain response over the first 3 months.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary **not met** for the pooled MR-HIFU arms vs EBRT; per-arm secondary trajectories are in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EBRT is the reference standard here, and the authors cite a 70% EBRT pain response; the EBRT arm reached 47% by wk 6. MR-HIFU has previously been tested mainly in pts failing or ineligible for RT, which is where the authors land their conclusion.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with painful non-spinal bone mets eligible for both EBRT and MR-HIFU. Does not represent spinal lesions, (impending) fracture, or life expectancy <3 months.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The 2-wk primary favors the faster-acting modality by design. The **pooled** MR-HIFU ± EBRT comparison blurs whether HIFU alone or the combination drives any difference. The EBRT arm underperformed the authors' own 70% benchmark.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The **26% → 81%** combination trajectory is the signal worth a confirmatory trial, but it is a secondary endpoint in an underpowered study. Low MR-HIFU eligibility is itself a finding: it caps how many pts the technique could reach.

studies.interpretation:
FURTHER asked a narrow question that matters to palliative RT practice: can MR-guided focused ultrasound, alone or added to EBRT, deliver pain relief faster and better than EBRT for non-spinal bone metastases? As reported, the trial cannot answer it. It randomized 69 of a planned 129 pts, and the prespecified comparison, both MR-HIFU arms pooled against EBRT at 2 weeks, gave 50% vs 38% with p = 0.41. Read straight, that is a missed primary. Leaning on the point estimate as evidence of benefit is the trap: with roughly half the intended sample, a difference of this size is compatible with no effect.

The endpoint choice deserves scrutiny in both directions. A 2-week timepoint is reasonable for a trial whose hypothesis is speed, and the authors say themselves that EBRT takes 4-6 weeks to act. It also stacks the comparison toward the ablative modality, so a null result on that endpoint is more damaging to the MR-HIFU-alone hypothesis than it first looks. The secondary trajectories support that reading: MR-HIFU alone went 47% at week 1 to 50% at week 6, a fast but flat response, while EBRT climbed from 35% to 47%.

The figure that will get quoted is the combination arm, rising from 26% to 81% over the same window. It is the most interesting number in the abstract and the least defended. It is a secondary endpoint in one arm of 23 pts, there is no reported test for it, and the low week-1 figure in that arm suggests the early benefit came from neither component. A real additive effect, where EBRT supplies durable response and HIFU supplies extra ablation, is biologically plausible. So is chance in a small arm.

Two gaps limit transfer to RT practice. EBRT dose and fractionation are not reported, so a reader cannot tell whether the control matched the single-fraction or multi-fraction regimens used in their clinic. And the EBRT arm reached 47% at week 6 against the 70% response the authors quote as the EBRT benchmark. A weak control flatters every comparison against it, so any apparent advantage for the HIFU arms should be discounted until the full paper shows the RT delivered.

The low MR-HIFU eligibility that sank accrual is a clinical finding in its own right: even if the technique works, it reaches a selected minority of pts. The defensible read is the authors' own conclusion, MR-HIFU as an option where EBRT is no longer available, plus a hypothesis that combination therapy deserves an adequately powered trial. The promised Bayesian analysis may sharpen probabilities, but it cannot recover the information lost to under-accrual.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The RT read is the combination arm: pain response rose 26% → 81% from wk 1 to wk 6 with EBRT then MR-HIFU vs 35% → 47% with EBRT alone. EBRT dose was not reported, and the decision in play is adding HIFU to EBRT, not replacing EBRT.

open_questions: Does EBRT plus MR-HIFU improve pain response in an adequately powered trial?
Which EBRT dose/fractionation was the comparator?
How many bone-met pts are MR-HIFU eligible in practice?

sites.intro: Two negative IO + dCRT esophageal readouts sit beside a positive local-control signal for adding SBRT in pancreas.

studies.name: ARION PRODIGE 67
studies.tldr: Adding durvalumab to definitive CRT did not improve 12-mo cPFS (48.6% vs 48.9%, HR 0.91) in locally advanced esophageal cancer.

details.text: 📊 Efficacy at 24-mo follow-up, CRT + durvalumab vs CRT alone

details: 🔍 Open-label randomized phase II, N=112 (58 vs 54), 13 French sites
☢️ RT backbone fixed both arms: IMRT 50 Gy/25 fx over 5 wk + 6 cycles FOLFOX
💊 Durvalumab 1500 mg monthly × 12 added to CRT in the experimental arm
🔍 Primary endpoint centrally reviewed PFS; 74 events to detect HR 0.55, 90% power, 10% one-sided alpha
🔍 Median age 67, 68% male, 77% SCC, 70% node-positive
⚠️ Powered only for HR 0.55; a modest benefit cannot be excluded
⚠️ Treatment-related AEs higher with durvalumab; G≥3 AE rates similar
⚠️ No locoregional control or pattern-of-failure data reported in source
🔗 Direction matches KUNLUN (durvalumab + dCRT in ESCC), also reported negative

verdict.rationale: Randomized, primary endpoint missed with HR near 1 across cPFS, PFS and OS; reinforces dCRT alone. Small phase II powered only for HR 0.55.
verdict.audience: Non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable ADK, PS ≤1

studies.significance: The RT backbone is the transferable part: IMRT 50 Gy/25 fx with FOLFOX, the European dCRT standard, so the null applies directly to Western practice. No locoregional failure data are reported, so whether durvalumab changed in-field control is unknown; the OS rate gap (75.1% vs 67.9%) carries HR 0.99.
studies.monday_clinic: In non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma treated with definitive 50 Gy/25 fx plus FOLFOX, this does not support adding durvalumab; it does not address adjuvant IO after trimodality resection.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicentric **open-label randomized phase II**, 13 French sites, May 2019 to May 2024. Stratified by tumor stage, histology and center; analysis after **24-month follow-up**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Age ≥18, **WHO PS ≤1**, **non-metastatic locally advanced SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma**. Median age 67, 77% SCC, 70% nodal extension.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **IMRT 50 Gy/25 daily fractions over 5 weeks**, identical in both arms, with 6 cycles of FOLFOX.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Arm A added **durvalumab 1500 mg monthly × 12** to CRT; arm B CRT alone. FOLFOX: oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, leucovorin 200 mg/m2, 5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus then 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** centrally reviewed PFS, 74 events to detect HR 0.55 (90% power, 10% one-sided alpha). Secondary: OS, PFS, safety.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Treatment-related AEs **higher with durvalumab**; G≥3 AE rates similar. No new safety signal.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Consistent with **KUNLUN**, the durvalumab plus dCRT trial in ESCC, also reported negative. Adjuvant IO after trimodality therapy (CheckMate 577) is a different setting and is not tested here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma receiving definitive 50 Gy/25 fx plus FOLFOX. Does not represent resectable disease on a trimodality path or pts with PS ≥2.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Wide CIs (cPFS HR upper bound 1.49) and a liberal one-sided alpha; histology too SCC-weighted to read adenocarcinoma separately. No PD-L1 or other predictive data yet.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Concurrent PD-L1 blockade **adds toxicity without PFS or OS gain** over dCRT at 24 months. Mature OS and predictive factors are pending, so a biomarker-selected benefit stays open.

studies.interpretation:
The case for adding PD-1/PD-L1 blockade to definitive chemoradiotherapy in esophageal cancer rested on two arguments: checkpoint inhibitors extend survival in the metastatic setting, and RT might prime an immune response that concurrent blockade could exploit. ARION is the first randomized test of that idea on a Western backbone, and it found nothing. All three efficacy endpoints sit near unity (cPFS HR 0.91, PFS HR 0.92, OS HR 0.99), with 12-month cPFS of 48.6% vs 48.9%. The direction matches KUNLUN, the durvalumab plus dCRT trial in ESCC, which was also reported negative. Two independent negative trials of the same drug in the same concurrent setting make the priming argument hard to sustain for unselected pts.

The main reason for caution is statistical. The trial was sized to detect HR 0.55, an effect larger than checkpoint inhibitors usually produce in any esophageal setting, and it used a one-sided alpha of 10%. A design like that can surface a large signal; it cannot rule out a modest one. The 12-month OS rates (75.1% vs 67.9%) look like a gap, but the HR of 0.99 and an interval running to 1.68 say the curves are not separating in any way the data can support. Over-reading that rate difference would be a mistake.

For the radiation oncologist, the backbone is what matters. Both arms received IMRT 50 Gy/25 fx with FOLFOX, the standard European dCRT, so the result applies to Western practice in a way the Asian ESCC trials do not fully cover. The trial doesn't tell us whether durvalumab changed in-field control: the abstract reports no locoregional failure or pattern-of-failure data, and those would be the most informative secondary read for whether immune blockade does anything at the irradiated site.

The population was 77% SCC, so an adenocarcinoma-specific effect cannot be judged, and no PD-L1 or other predictive data are given yet. A biomarker-selected benefit is still possible and is the obvious next question. ARION leaves adjuvant IO after trimodality resection untouched; that is a separate setting with its own evidence. For unselected pts on definitive 50 Gy with FOLFOX, concurrent and maintenance durvalumab adds treatment-related toxicity without measurable gain, and CRT alone remains the standard against which any future combination must be tested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: IMRT 50 Gy/25 fx with FOLFOX was identical in both arms, so this tests IO added to a transferable dCRT backbone, not RT itself. No local control or pattern-of-failure data reported, leaving the in-field effect of durvalumab unknown.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Twelve monthly 1500 mg durvalumab doses added to dCRT did not move cPFS, PFS or OS (HRs 0.91, 0.92, 0.99). Benefit of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in the metastatic setting did not carry into concurrent definitive therapy; biomarker selection remains unreported.

open_questions: Predictive biomarker for IO benefit with definitive CRT
Effect in adenocarcinoma given SCC-dominant enrollment

studies.name: AGITG MASTERPLAN
studies.tldr: 12mth LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (p=0.022) adding SBRT 40Gy/5fx to 3mths mFOLFIRINOX-based CT in high-risk operable, BRPC or LAPC.
details: 🔍 Randomised phase II, 2:1 CT+SBRT (I) vs CT alone (C), 14 sites, 75 enrolled, 1 ineligible
🔍 48 POPC (high-risk operable + BRPC) and 26 IPC (LAPC / medically inoperable); central radiology review
💊 CT clinician choice: mFOLFIRINOX 90-92%, gem/nab-paclitaxel in the remainder; 3mths before surgical evaluation
🔍 SBRT 40Gy in 5 fractions, fiducial marker guidance, real-time RT quality assurance

details.text: 📊 Outcomes by arm (I n=49, C n=25)
📊 Surgical outcomes, POPC only (I n=31, C n=17)

details: ⚠️ Only 39 (80%) of the SBRT arm commenced SBRT; 2 (4%) withdrew before CT
⚠️ OS and PFS are secondary endpoints in a 74-pt trial; OS signal is hypothesis-generating
⚠️ Baseline imbalances: male 72% (C) vs 51% (I), p=0.08; median Ca19.9 340 (C) vs 180 (I)
⚠️ IPC stratum (n=26) underpowered; LRR difference there not significant (p=0.16)
⚠️ Abstract only; registered ACTRN12619000409178, no NCT

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase II met its 1° EP, but N=74, a 12mth local endpoint, OS as a secondary, abstract-only data and baseline imbalances need phase III confirmation.
verdict.audience: High-risk operable, borderline resectable or locally advanced pancreatic cancer

studies.significance: The local control benefit held although only 39 (80%) of the SBRT arm actually commenced SBRT, delivered as 40Gy/5fx with fiducials and real-time QA. The benefit is clearest in POPC (12mth LRR 19.7% vs 52.9%, p=0.031). That puts SBRT inside induction CT back in play for BRPC.
studies.monday_clinic: In borderline resectable or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer on induction mFOLFIRINOX, this supports SBRT within the induction window as a local-control option worth trial-level discussion; it does not settle LAPC, where the LRR difference was not significant.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomised phase II**, 2:1 to 3mths CT+SBRT vs 3mths CT alone, 14 sites. 75 enrolled, 1 ineligible; I n=49, C n=25.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Operable disease with **≥1 high-risk feature** (>4 cm, extrapancreatic extension or node positive), BRPC, or LAPC. 48 POPC and 26 IPC; staging per AGITG guidelines with central radiology review.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: CT by clinician choice, **mFOLFIRINOX in 92% (C) and 90% (I)**, otherwise gem/nab-paclitaxel. After resection, 3mths adjuvant CT; pts unsuitable for resection continued CT for a further 3mths.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 40Gy in 5 fractions** with fiducial marker guidance and real-time RT quality assurance, given during the 3mth induction period. **SBRT commenced in 39 (80%)** of the investigational arm.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 12mth LRR.** Secondary: resection rate, margin status, CTCAE v5.0 toxicity, PFS and OS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade 3+ toxicity **70.2% (I) vs 64.0% (C), p=0.27**, so SBRT added no measurable grade 3+ toxicity at this sample size.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PREOPANC and the Alliance borderline-resectable trial tested preoperative RT strategies that did not establish RT as standard with modern multiagent induction. MASTERPLAN differs by pairing 5-fraction SBRT with mFOLFIRINOX and choosing a local primary endpoint.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk operable, borderline resectable and locally advanced pancreatic cancer receiving mostly mFOLFIRINOX induction. Does not represent operable disease without a high-risk feature.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Baseline imbalances in sex (72% vs 51% male, p=0.08) and Ca19.9 (median 340 vs 180) with control the higher-risk-looking arm. The R0 gain (62% vs 40%) is not significant (p=0.44) on 31 resections.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The local control result is the solid finding, and the PFS and OS signals point the same way. Whether halving 12mth LRR carries an OS benefit in a disease driven by distant failure needs a larger trial.

studies.interpretation:
The question MASTERPLAN asks is whether local therapy still earns a place in pancreatic cancer now that multiagent induction chemotherapy has become the backbone. The trials that shaped current practice, including PREOPANC and the Alliance borderline-resectable study, left radiotherapy looking optional at best once mFOLFIRINOX entered the picture. MASTERPLAN reframes the question in two ways. It uses a short, high-dose SBRT course that fits inside the induction window, so pts do not lose systemic therapy time. It also makes locoregional recurrence the primary endpoint, measuring the thing radiotherapy can plausibly change rather than asking a local therapy to prove itself on survival from the outset.

On that endpoint the result is clear: 12mth LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (p=0.022), with the control arm's local failure rate high enough to show how much residual locoregional disease mFOLFIRINOX leaves behind. The stratum results matter for transfer. The POPC effect (19.7% vs 52.9%, p=0.031) is where the evidence sits. The IPC point estimates (21.4% vs 50.0%) look similar, but 26 pts and p=0.16 do not support a separate claim for LAPC.

The secondary signals should be read with more caution than the abstract's conclusion invites. Median OS 22.0 vs 14.0 mths (p=0.006) in a 74-pt phase II, as a secondary endpoint, is the kind of result that tends to shrink in a confirmatory trial. The direction of the baseline imbalances matters too: the control arm had more men (72% vs 51%) and a higher median Ca19.9 (340 vs 180). Neither reached significance, but at this sample size, chance imbalances in prognostic factors can account for part of a survival gap. Distant progression drives most pancreatic cancer deaths, so an OS effect this large from a local intervention would need a mechanism (better resectability, fewer locoregional complications, or local control preventing reseeding) that the abstract cannot yet show.

Two features argue the local control effect is real and not inflated. First, only 80% of the SBRT arm started SBRT, so the intention-to-treat comparison already includes pts who never got the intervention. Second, SBRT added no measurable grade 3+ toxicity (70.2% vs 64.0%, p=0.27), which removes the usual cost argument against adding RT. The surgical data lean the same way without proving anything: resection 68% vs 59% and R0 62% vs 40% in POPC, both non-significant on small denominators.

What would make this wrong? A phase III in which the LRR benefit holds but survival does not separate would make SBRT a local-control and morbidity tool rather than a survival intervention. That would still be clinically useful, but it is a different recommendation. The 40Gy/5fx regimen with fiducials and real-time QA is also a protocol-level technique, and the result may not carry over to less precise delivery or lower doses. Until a confirmatory trial reports, this is the strongest randomised argument for SBRT during mFOLFIRINOX induction in borderline resectable disease, and a weaker one for LAPC.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 40Gy/5fx SBRT with fiducials and real-time QA cut 12mth LRR to 20.2% vs 52.0%, with the effect clearest in POPC (19.7% vs 52.9%, p=0.031). The benefit held although only 80% of the SBRT arm started SBRT, which puts SBRT inside induction CT back in play for BRPC.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: SBRT fits within the 3mth mFOLFIRINOX induction without losing CT time, and grade 3+ toxicity was 70.2% vs 64.0% (p=0.27). PFS 11.9 vs 6.3 mths and OS 22.0 vs 14.0 mths are secondary signals in 74 pts and need phase III confirmation before they change sequencing.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: In POPC, resection was 68% vs 59% (p=0.54) and R0 (>1mm) 62% vs 40% (p=0.44) with SBRT. Neither difference is significant on 31 resections, but SBRT did not compromise operability after induction, and the margin trend is worth tracking in a larger trial.

open_questions: Does the OS signal hold in a phase III?
Does SBRT benefit LAPC, or only potentially operable disease?
Does SBRT improve R0 resection rates with adequate power?

studies.name: KEYNOTE-975
studies.tldr: EFS HR 0.97 (0.77-1.23), 15.2 vs 14.7 mo in CPS ≥10: pembrolizumab added to dCRT failed its primary endpoint in unresectable esophageal/GEJ cancer.
details: 🔍 Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, international; N=703 assigned 1:1 (349 pembro vs 354 placebo)
🔍 Untreated locally advanced ESCC, EAC or GEJ; ECOG 0-1; ineligible for curative surgery, suitable for dCRT

details.text: 📊 Efficacy in PD-L1 CPS ≥10, second interim analysis (median f/u 47.1 mo)

details: 📐 EFS CPS ≥10 failure stopped hierarchical testing: CPS ≥1, overall population EFS and OS not formally tested
🔍 Study stopped after this analysis

details.text: 📊 Safety, pembro + dCRT vs placebo + dCRT

details: ⚠️ RT dose not standardized: 50 or 60 Gy with FP, 50 Gy with FOLFOX, at investigator choice
⚠️ EFS investigator-assessed; no histology (ESCC vs EAC) breakdown in source
⚠️ No locoregional control or pattern-of-failure data in source

verdict.rationale: Randomized double-blind phase 3 with mature 47.1-mo f/u; hierarchical primary EFS in CPS ≥10 missed and trial stopped. Reaffirms dCRT without IO as reference.
verdict.audience: Untreated unresectable esophageal/GEJ cancer, dCRT-eligible, ECOG 0-1

studies.significance: The RT read: pembrolizumab added nothing to dCRT across all three backbones (FP with 50 or 60 Gy, FOLFOX with 50 Gy), while fatal AEs ran 13% vs 10%. Whether IO changed in-field control is unknown, since locoregional and pattern-of-failure data are not reported in source. The dCRT backbone stays unchanged for unresectable disease.
studies.monday_clinic: In untreated unresectable esophageal or GEJ cancer with PD-L1 CPS ≥10 going to definitive CRT, this does not support adding concurrent and maintenance pembrolizumab; it does not address resected disease after neoadjuvant CRT, a setting this trial did not test.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International **randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3**, 1:1, N=703 (349 vs 354). Results from the **second interim analysis**, data cutoff January 21, 2026, median follow-up **47.1 mo**. Study stopped after this analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Previously untreated, locally advanced **ESCC, EAC or GEJ cancer**, ECOG 0-1, **ineligible for curative surgery** but suitable for dCRT. Primary analysis population was **PD-L1 CPS ≥10**.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3w for 8 cycles, then 400 mg q6w for 5 cycles, vs matching placebo. Chemotherapy was investigator-selected fluorouracil plus cisplatin, or FOLFOX.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **50 or 60 Gy** with fluorouracil/cisplatin, or **50 Gy** with FOLFOX. Fractionation, technique and target volume not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Dual primary:** investigator-assessed EFS and OS, evaluated in CPS ≥10, CPS ≥1 and the overall population. Hierarchical testing started with EFS in CPS ≥10.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **EFS in CPS ≥10 not met**, so formal testing of the remaining endpoints did not proceed. OS in CPS ≥10 showed **no apparent benefit**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade ≥3 AEs in **100%** of both arms. Fatal AEs **13% vs 10%** and AE discontinuation **34% vs 27%**, both higher with pembrolizumab. No new safety signals reported.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The result breaks from settings where checkpoint inhibition adds to CRT, such as PACIFIC consolidation in stage III NSCLC and CheckMate 577 adjuvant nivolumab after neoadjuvant CRT and resection in esophageal cancer. Here IO was given concurrently and as maintenance with nonoperative dCRT, and that combination failed.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents untreated unresectable esophageal or GEJ cancer treated with definitive CRT, PD-L1 CPS ≥10. Does not represent resected disease after neoadjuvant CRT, or the CPS ≥1 and all-comer populations, which were not formally tested.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: EFS was **investigator-assessed**, not centrally reviewed. RT dose varied by investigator choice (50 vs 60 Gy) and ESCC and adenocarcinoma were pooled; no histology-specific results in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Concurrent-plus-maintenance pembrolizumab did not convert into EFS or OS gains, and fatal toxicity trended higher. What stays open is whether a different IO timing (consolidation after dCRT) or a histology-selected population behaves differently.

studies.interpretation:
KEYNOTE-975 is a clean negative. It was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, and with median follow-up of 47.1 months the EFS curves in the CPS ≥10 population had plenty of time to separate. They did not: HR 0.97 with an interval spanning 0.77 to 1.23, and OS HR 1.00. Calling this the second interim analysis should not be read as immaturity in the usual sense. A trial with this much follow-up and a point estimate this close to unity is not a result waiting for more events. The sponsor stopped the study, and that decision fits the data.

The result matters because enrichment logic said it should have worked. Selecting CPS ≥10 was a bet that PD-L1 expression would identify the pts most likely to gain from IO layered on radiation, the reasoning behind PACIFIC in stage III NSCLC and CheckMate 577 in resected esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant CRT. In the nonoperative esophageal setting that reasoning did not hold. One plausible explanation is timing. KEYNOTE-975 gave pembrolizumab concurrently with dCRT and then as maintenance, while both positive comparators added IO after locoregional treatment was finished. The trial cannot tell concurrent toxicity apart from a true lack of synergy, but the safety data point somewhere. Fatal AEs were 13% vs 10% and AE discontinuation 34% vs 27%, so pts on the experimental arm were more likely to stop therapy and more likely to die of toxicity, which could absorb any efficacy gain.

For a radiation oncologist, the design choices limit what the trial says about RT itself. Dose was investigator-selected, 50 or 60 Gy with FP or 50 Gy with FOLFOX, and the source reports no locoregional control or patterns of failure. So it is unknown whether pembrolizumab changed in-field control while failing systemically, or did nothing at either level. Pooling squamous and adenocarcinoma histologies adds another layer of heterogeneity, given how differently the two behave after CRT; a histology split is not in the source. EFS was also investigator-assessed, but an unblinded-assessment bias would usually push toward the experimental arm, so it does not explain a null.

What the trial settles: concurrent-plus-maintenance pembrolizumab, on this schedule, should not be added to dCRT for unresectable esophageal or GEJ cancer with CPS ≥10. What it leaves open: whether consolidation-only IO after dCRT, a squamous-only population, or a less toxic chemotherapy backbone would perform differently, and whether CPS is the right selector in a field already given an RT-induced immune stimulus. Because the hierarchy stopped at the first endpoint, nothing should be inferred about CPS ≥1 or all-comers in either direction. For now dCRT alone remains the reference arm any future IO trial in this setting has to beat.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: IO added nothing to dCRT across FP with 50 or 60 Gy and FOLFOX with 50 Gy, so the RT backbone and its dose choices stay as they are. Locoregional control and failure patterns are not reported in source, so any in-field effect of pembrolizumab is unknown.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Concurrent-plus-maintenance pembrolizumab failed even in the CPS ≥10 enriched group (EFS HR 0.97, OS HR 1.00), while fatal AEs (13% vs 10%) and discontinuation (34% vs 27%) rose. CPS selection did not rescue IO in the nonoperative setting, and the CPS ≥1 and all-comer populations were never formally tested.

open_questions: Does consolidation-only IO after dCRT outperform concurrent dosing?
Differential effect in ESCC vs adenocarcinoma?
Locoregional control and failure patterns with IO added?

papers.title: Randomised phase II study of mFOLFIRINOX ± SBRT in patients with high risk, borderline resectable or locally advanced pancreatic cancer: Results of the AGITG MASTERPLAN trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3136RO · Rapid oral 1: Gastrointestinal tumour, upper digestive · 2026-10-23 · presented by Andrew Oar (Southport, Australia)

Background: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) delivers high-dose, precision radiotherapy (RT). Despite advances in chemotherapy (CT) for pancreatic cancer (PC), locoregional recurrences (LRR) are frequent and contribute to morbidity/mortality.
Methods: Eligible pts had operable disease with ≥1 high risk feature (>4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, or node positive), or BRPC, or LAPC. High-risk operable and BRPC pts were classified as potentially operable PC (POPC), while LAPC/medically inoperable pts as inoperable PC (IPC). Staging followed AGITG guidelines with central radiology review. CT was clinician choice: mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel. Pts were randomised 2:1 to 3mths of CT+SBRT (I) or to 3mths CT alone (C). SBRT was 40Gy in 5 fractions with fiducial marker guidance and real time RT quality assurance. After CT±SBRT, pts were evaluated for surgery. Following resection pts received 3mths adjuvant CT. Pts unsuitable for resection, continued CT for further 3mths. The primary endpoint was 12mth LRR. Secondary endpoints included resection rate, margin status, toxicity per CTCAE (v5.0), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS).
Results: Across 14 sites 75 pts were enrolled with 1 ineligible, including 48 POPC and 26 IPC. 12mth LRR rates were 20.2 % (95% CI: 9.9-33.2%) v 52.0% (95% CI: 30.3-69.9%) in I and C respectively (p=0.022). In POPC, 12mth LRR rates were 19.7% (95% CI: 7.8–35.6) (I) v 52.9% (95% CI: 25.9–74.1) (C) (p=0.031), and in IPC 21.4% (95% CI: 4.8–45.8) (I) v 50.0% (95% CI: 11.4-80.2) (C) (p=0.16). Overall Grade 3+ toxicity occurred in 70.2% (I) and 64.0% (C) (p=0.27). Median PFS was 11.9 v 6.3 mths (p=0.002) and median OS 22.0 v 14.0 mths (p=0.006) in I and C, respectively. Conclusions: SBRT improved LRR and PFS without additional toxicity. A significant OS signal was observed in this cohort. Further research to optimise the role of SBRT is required.

papers.title: A new fast-acting treatment option for painful bone metastases: A confirmatory trial of palliative arterial embolization assessing immediate efficacy and safety (PALEM Trial)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3087RO · Rapid oral: Supportive and palliative care · 2026-10-25 · presented by Yasunori Arai (Kashiwa, Japan)

Background: Painful bone metastases impair quality of life in patients with cancer, yet few options beyond analgesics provide relief within days. Palliative arterial embolization may enable rapid pain control by embolizing tumor-feeding vessels. We prospectively evaluated its immediate efficacy and safety.
Methods: The PALEM trial was a multicenter, single-arm, prospective confirmatory hypothesis-assessment study conducted under national palliative trial standards (J-SUPPORT policy). This protocol has been published. Eligible patients [on analgesics; Pain score ≥5; radiotherapy (RT)-ineligible or ≥8 weeks after prior RT] underwent embolization for the most painful lesion using microsphere, without anticancer drugs. The co-primary endpoints were immediate efficacy and safety. Immediate efficacy was defined by international consensus criteria for palliative RT trials, incorporating pain scores and daily morphine-equivalent doses. Pain score (Brief pain Inventory - short form item 3) was assessed at 72 h. Efficasy was defined as (a) reduced pain score with reduced opioid dose, (b) reduced pain score with unchanged opioid dose, or (c) unchanged pain score with reduced opioid dose. Immediate efficacy was evaluated by testing whether the efficasy rate exceeded 26% (one-sided α=0.025, 1−β=0.9), assuming a 40% response. Safety was defined as the incidence, through day 14, of embolization-related adverse events (any Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Event grade ≥4 event or grade ≥3 central nervous system necrosis). We tested whether the adverse event rate was <15% (one-sided α=0.025, 1−β=0.9). Overall success required both immediate efficacy and safety criteria be met.
Results: A total of 120 patients were enrolled. Immediate efficacy was achieved for 62 of 118 evaluable patients, yielding a 52.5% pain-relief rate (95% CI, 43.1–61.8%). The safety analysis set included 119 patients; no primary safety events occurred (95% CI, 0.0–3.1%). The trial met both primary endpoints.
Conclusions: The PALEM trial confirmed palliative arterial embolization as a valid treatment for painful bone metastases, providing immediate pain relief with acceptable safety.
Clinical trial identification: UMIN-CTR ID: UMIN000040794 release date: 2020/07/01.

papers.title: MRI-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound versus external beam radiotherapy for painful bone metastases: The FURTHER RCT
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3084O · Proffered paper: Supportive and palliative care · 2026-10-26 · presented by Manon Braat (Utrecht, Netherlands) · NCT04307914

Background: External beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is the standard of treatment for patients with painful bone metastases. Its effect takes 4-6 weeks to occur and 70% of patients achieve pain response. MRI-guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (MR-HIFU) is proposed as alternative or addition to EBRT. The multicenter FURTHER RCT investigated whether MR-HIFU, with or without EBRT, induces earlier and better pain response in patients with painful bone metastases.
Methods: Patients were enrolled between 2020-2025 in six European hospitals. Patients were adults with good/reasonable performance, painful (NRS ≥ 4) non-spinal bone metastases, eligible for EBRT and MR-HIFU. Patients with life expectancy <3 months, (impending) fracture, or curative treatment intent were excluded. Patients were 1:1:1 randomized to MR-HIFU, EBRT, or the combination (EBRT followed by MR-Hifu within one week). Primary endpoint was pain response two weeks following start of treatment based on pain score and opioid use as collected by the Brief Pain Inventory. Secondary endpoints included pain scores and pain response over the first three months.
Results: Despite 2 year project extention, the target sample size of 129 patients was not reached due COVID-19 and lower-than-expected MR-HIFU eligibility. 69 patients were randomized to MR-HIFU (n=22), combination treatment (n=23) and EBRT (n=24). Two weeks after the start of treatment, pain response was higher for MR-HIFU (with or without EBRT) than for EBRT; the difference was not statistically significant (50% vs. 38%, p = 0.41). In the first 2 weeks following start of treatment, pain scores dropped 2.3 points in the EBRT arm, 3.7 points in the combination arm, and 3.6 points in the MR- HIFU arm. Between 1-6 weeks following start of treatment, pain response increased from 35% to 47% for EBRT, from 26% to 81% for the combination treatment and from 47% to 50% for MR- HIFU.
Conclusions: MR- HIFU is effective for palliation of painful bone metastases and can be considered in patients for whom EBRT is no (longer an) option. Combining EBRT with MR- HIFU may lead to a higher pain response than current standard treatment. Bayesian analyses to mitigate the study's low power and improve its interpretability will be presented at ESMO.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04307914.

papers.title: Durvalumab plus definitive chemoradiotherapy versus definitive chemoradiotherapy in patients with locally advanced esophagus carcinoma: ARION PRODIGE 67 randomized phase 2 trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 2879RO · Rapid oral 1: Gastrointestinal tumour, upper digestive · 2026-10-23 · presented by Marie-Anouchka Modesto (Toulouse, France) · NCT03777813

Background: In locally advanced or unresectable esophageal cancer, definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is the standard of care (SoC) combining radiotherapy with platinum-based chemotherapy, resulting in a 2-year disease-free survival of 25%, which remains an unmet medical need. As immune checkpoint inhibitors increase survival in the metastatic setting, a multicentric, this open-label, comparative phase II ARION trial was designed to assess efficacy and safety of PD1/PDL1 blockade by durvalumab (D) added to SoC.
Methods: Patients (pts) ≥18 years old, WHO performance status ≤1, non-metastatic, locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or unresectable adenocarcinoma (ADK), (stratified by tumor stage, histology, centers) were randomized between arm A with 12 monthly 1500 mg (D) infusions added to SoC (IMRT 50 Gy/25 daily fractions over 5 weeks) and 6 cycles of FOLFOX regimen: oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, Leucovorin 200 mg/m2, 5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus then continuous 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h) or arm B (SoC). Primary endpoint was centrally reviewed progression-free survival (cPFS). Overall survival (OS), PFS and safety were secondary endpoints. 74 cPFS events were required to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.55 with 90% power (10% one-sided alpha).
Results: Between May 2019 and May 2024, 112 pts were randomized (Arm A: SoC + D, n=58 / Arm B: SoC, n=54) in 13 French sites. Analysis was performed after a 24-month follow-up. Median age was 67 years, 68% were male, 77% were SCC, 70% had nodal extension. There was no significant difference between arms for cPFS, PFS and OS (table). Treatment-related adverse events (AE) were higher in arm A. Grade ≥ 3 AE rates were similar in both arms. Table: 2879RO Arm A (exp) 12-month rate [95%CI] Arm B (SoC) 12-month rate [95%CI] Adjusted HR* [95%CI] [80%CI] 1-sided p-value cPFS 48.6% [34.6; 61.3] 48.9% [34.7; 61.7] 0.91 [0.55; 1.49] [0.66; 1.25] 0.351 PFS 50.1% [36.2; 62.5] 48.1% [33.7; 61.2] 0.92 [0.56; 1.50] [0.67; 1.27] 0.369 OS 75.1% [61.6; 84.4] 67.9% [53.6; 78.7] 0.99 [0.59; 1.68] [0.70; 1.40] 0.489 *for Histological subtype, Stage
Conclusions: In this indication, Durvalumab with CRT compared to SoC did not improve PFS. There was no new safety signal. Longer survival, follow-up and predictive factors for treatment efficacy will be presented.
Clinical trial identification: NCT03777813.
